items: Warnings has a place of its own, opened from the plan: the Warnings button at the top of the plan’s side buttons shows how many there are to look at (a gray check when none are found), and it’s also in ⋮ and in Settings. Each kind says what it checks, and one that can’t run yet (no ZIP, no kids or pets chosen, no sun area) says what it needs, with a button to set it.

On a phone, choose a warning and the plan zooms to its plants, with “Warnings · 3 of 12” at the bottom to go to the next one, dismiss it, or go back to the list. On a computer, Warnings stays open beside the plan while you work through it.

A Plant list: what to buy, what’s planted and what was there already, a line for each kind with its variety, botanical name, how many, its size and which beds. Open it with the list button beside Through the year, or from ⋮. Tick each kind as you buy it: the ticks go with the plan to your other devices. Once bought, Mark planted records the day they go in, with Undo. Share or copy the list as text, or print it in big type.

Who’s in the yard (kids, dogs, cats, horses) and which warnings are switched on in Warnings are now kept with each plan, not each device: they go with the plan to your other devices and into backups, and opening another plan switches to that plan’s. Your plans keep what you had set. A new plan starts with every warning on and asks “Anyone you need to protect?” again, unless you keep “Same garden?” ticked.

An empty plan now has a box for your garden’s ZIP right on it: it gives the garden’s hardiness zone, frost dates and your state’s plant laws. On a new device it also says what FullGrown does, and “Restore a backup” brings in plans you saved on another device.

An empty plan's first screen now sits on a card, with an ✕ that puts it away for that plan. Once the plan has a photo, the card moves to the bottom, above the buttons, so the photo shows and the words stay easy to read.

“Privacy”, at the end of the ZIP box's note, opens the garden's location, which now says plainly what happens to your ZIP: looking it up sends only its first three digits, and the ZIP is kept with the plan, on this device, in backups, and in your account if you sign in to sync.

In the plant picker, words of what you need become filters as you type: “shade flowers” sets Part shade and Has flowers, a new filter under Looks. Sun and shade, evergreen, native, deer, wet, dry, clay, a kind of plant (shrub, tree, vine…) and a flower color (“blue flowers”) all work. A word that’s part of a plant’s name, as in Deer fern, stays in the search.
Typing a search in the plant picker folds the open filters away, so the results are in view; “Add as my plant” is now a link under the results.

Each plant in the plant picker shows its bloom months (“Jun–Aug”) where they’re known, and its color spot is now a small flower in its flowers’ color inside a circle of its leaves’ color; a plant without showy flowers shows just the circle.

Plants blooming in a month you choose: those with months for it come first, and those whose sources give only a season are folded below, saying why. Your ZIP adds months from flowering records near the garden.
The plant picker’s “In this plan” now counts your plants (“16 plants, 7 kinds”, and × 4 on each kind), and the Bloom calendar shows each plant’s whole name, its variety included.

The plant picker asks “Anyone you need to protect?” before its other filters: choose Kids, Dogs, Cats or Horses, and plants that are a problem for them are hidden and flagged on your plan. Plants that can irritate skin are marked for everyone, since anyone can brush them. Once you’ve answered or closed it, it’s under Filters → Poison & pets.

Which plants count as flowering now follows the same rule everywhere, the one a plant's details use: flowers its sources call insignificant (oaks, boxwood, grasses and the like) aren't counted under a flower color or as blooming on the calendar, and plants whose showy parts are bracts, like Flowering dogwood, now are.

One word for it everywhere: Dismiss, and Show again. A plant’s details offer “Dismiss for this one” or “Dismiss for every” plant of its kind, and a dismissed warning says which. The hardiness notice’s Leave it is gone (its ✕ closes it), and the crowding notice’s Leave it is now Dismiss.

In Warnings, Dismiss beside a warning works as it does from the plant (hardiness, poison and fruit partners go for every copy of that plant in the plan), a dismissed one says who it’s dismissed for, and with more than one of a kind, Dismiss all and Show all again take care of them at once, with an Undo. For crowding they take the place of Leave all flagged now and Flag them again.

With Layers showing only some plants, Warnings says only those are checked, with Show all plants, instead of saying there’s nothing to look at; its button then shows the warning sign in gray, not the all-clear check.
Warnings read as a plant’s details do: poison with how severe it is, sun naming the sun area, a tree’s height in whole feet.

A plant’s details now say what the law says of it in South Carolina, New York and Massachusetts too, and Michigan’s 2026 additions are in: Callery pear, Japanese barberry and two buckthorns, which Michigan restricts from 2028.
Deleting a bed with plants in it asks whether its plants go too or stay (with locked plants in it: all of them, only the unlocked ones, or none), and deleting a project offers to save a copy first.
A plant you copy as your own is ready to place once it's saved, as one you add is. Copied in Switch plant, while placing, it becomes the plant you're placing.
Copy as my plant starts with the name empty and no flower colors picked, for you to fill in; size, sun, type and bloom come from the catalog plant.
A copy of a catalog plant is drawn with the original's leaves through the year: a copied conifer stays evergreen, with needles.
A plant of your own with no flower colors and no bloom months is drawn without flowers, rather than with flowers in its plan color.
Butterfly weed ‘for Clay’ is now called Butterfly weed (clay strain): it’s a strain grown from seed, not a named variety. Its details are the same, and a search for its old name still finds it.
A Water iris already on your plan is now Blue flag iris, a native iris whose details come from checked sources. It keeps its spot, size and label there.
A new plan can start with your garden’s location: New project offers “Same garden (ZIP …)?”, already ticked.
The plan’s name at the top now looks like the button it is (it opens your plans), with Saved under it; ⋮ also has Plans and backup….
⋮ → the version line has Check for updates: if a new version is ready, it says so, and Update now switches to it, your work saved first.
Closing Swap, Add a plant or the ZIP box opened from the plant picker now takes you back where you were, instead of out to the plan, and its ← in place of × says so.
While a sheet is open, Undo and Redo at the top are grayed out and do nothing; before, they closed the sheet with your change still in place. Close it first, then Undo.
A panel, menu or question that has just come up ignores presses for a moment, so pressing twice quickly no longer sets off whatever came up under your finger.
A sun exposure area no longer gets in the way of what’s on it: a plant is picked first, then the bed, then the sun area.
Typing a building’s sides on a phone: the second side goes toward the middle of the screen, the building stays in view, and the typed length shows by its corner with what to do next.
Zooming, moving around the plan or Fit no longer counts as a change, so Projects shows when you last changed the plan itself.
Files you save (backups, plan files, pictures, the PDF) are dated by your own calendar: late in the evening they no longer carry tomorrow’s date.
Printing and pictures: bed names are no longer hidden under plants or printed over another name, and a picture of the plan has Download and, where your device can, Share….
On a computer, point at Undo or Redo to see what it would do: “Undo: delete Front bed”.

The bar at the bottom should no longer end up partly off the screen after an update (the app now measures the screen when it starts and whenever you come back to it), and a rare blank screen while reading a plant’s details is fixed.
The pins marking plants hidden under bigger ones shrink sooner as you zoom out and are gone below 85%, and they’re hidden along with names and badges.

Smaller fixes: “Which tree?” starts with no filters; a plant you swap in shows first under Recent; the plant picker’s title and count agree; a plant copied from the catalog isn’t flagged as “now in the catalog”; several plants selected are named as plants; the dashed ring around a plant is explained as its full size; the new-version message sits under the top bar instead of over the plan’s buttons; an old message clears when you start drawing; a bed’s bloom chart no longer runs its numbers together; back on a plan after another, Redo no longer offers a change undone before you left; and on a computer the ZIP box opens with the cursor in it.
On a computer, the app’s instructions now speak of the mouse, not of a touch screen.
Through the year: a plant in the list of what’s in bloom selects those plants on the plan, and the month stays.
Print: after Create, its last options are no longer hidden under the bar at the bottom.
Several plants selected on a small phone: the bar fits, its buttons shown as icons when space is short.
Layers counts every locked shape, locked on its own or with its layer, and a layer’s row says “1 locked shape” when a shape is locked on its own.
A vine on a fence or trellis: hiding that layer hides the vine’s band along it too; its planting spot and name stay.
The pins marking plants hidden under bigger ones shrink as you zoom out, and go away when you’re zoomed far out (below 30%) or the plant is only a speck; zoom in and they’re back.

A plant’s details now say what the law says of it in twelve more states, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois, North Carolina, Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, New Jersey, Alabama and West Virginia, read from each state’s own legal text. A plant your state bans is left out while you browse, as before.
A plant of your own: choose its flower colors as chips in its form, kept even without bloom months; its flowers are drawn in the first one chosen.
The plant picker’s filters have a Mature width slider beside Mature height: “up to 3 ft” finds plants that fit a narrow spot, with those that typically fit but can grow wider listed below them.
Settings has a sheet of its own: ⋮ → Settings. Text size, the size of names on the plan, drawing aids and warnings are all there.
Settings → Warnings → “In this plan now” lists every warning in the open plan, and can show again ones you dismissed.
Print starts from what the screen shows: the plants shown or hidden, names on or off, the month.

A plant’s details say when the U.S. Geological Survey lists it as invasive in the lower 48. A plant your state’s law bans is left out while you browse; a search still finds it, with a red “Place (banned)”.
Redo is easier to find: after an undo, it shows next to Undo.
A tree you draw that’s already in the yard is marked Existing, not Planted.
This list: after an update, a notice says what’s new; ⋮ → What’s new shows it any time.
